When something is afoot, it means it is currently happening, in progress, or being actively planned — especially when the thing in question feels significant, mysterious, or somewhat secretive.

Think of it like this: if "afoot" describes a situation, it means the gears are already turning. Something has been set in motion. The world is not sitting still — something is going on.

This is where "afoot" gets its personality, and it's important.

"Afoot" does not just mean happening. The word carries a sense of intrigue, suspicion, or quiet momentum. When someone says "something is afoot," they are usually hinting that:

  • They sense activity going on around them, possibly behind the scenes
  • Things may not be totally visible or confirmed yet, but the signs are there
  • The situation feels significant — not ordinary, not trivial

It is the kind of word you use when you suspect something, when you feel a shift in the air, when events seem to be moving in a particular direction — even if you cannot fully see them yet.

"Afoot" as an adjective is always a predicate adjective. This means it only appears after a linking verb (most commonly the verb to be: is, are, was, were). It describes the subject of the sentence.

✅ Correct:

  • Something is afoot.
  • Changes are afoot.
  • A plan was afoot.

❌ Incorrect:
You cannot place "afoot" directly before a noun like a regular adjective.

  • An afoot plan ✗
  • The afoot scheme ✗

This is a fixed rule. "Afoot" only works in the predicate position.

Let's walk through examples so you can feel how the word behaves:

1. "Something is afoot in this town."
The speaker senses unusual activity. People are behaving strangely. Events feel suspicious. Something significant is happening — possibly in secret.

2. "Major changes are afoot at the company."
Big restructuring, new leadership, or a policy overhaul is already underway. The process has begun and is moving forward.

3. "The detective sensed that mischief was afoot."
The detective suspected that someone was plotting something troublesome. The trouble hadn't fully revealed itself yet, but the signs were there.

4. "Plans are afoot to build a new hospital in the city."
The planning process is actively happening right now. Decisions are being made, meetings are being held — it is not just an idea; it is in motion.

5. "I don't know what is afoot, but the officers are all rushing around."
The speaker doesn't know the details but can clearly see that something is happening based on the behaviour around them.

The phrase "The game is afoot" was made legendary by the fictional detective Sherlock Holmes. When Holmes says this, he means: the hunt has begun; the investigation is now in active progress; it is time to move. It is a thrilling, energising declaration that something significant is now underway.

This is a perfect example of the word's spirit — urgency, momentum, a sense that things are no longer still.

Depending on the context, "afoot" can lean in slightly different emotional directions:

ContextShade of Meaning
Political or social newsNeutral — changes are simply in progress
Mystery or thrillerSuspicious — something secretive is happening
Adventure or actionExciting — things are beginning to move
Negative situationsOminous — something bad may be developing

Depending on context, "afoot" can feel neutral (changes are simply happening), suspicious (something secretive is going on), exciting (an adventure is beginning), or even ominous (something bad may be developing). The word itself is flexible — the surrounding context shapes its emotional weight.
How It Differs from Similar Words

"Underway" — Also means in progress, but it sounds more neutral and practical. "The construction is underway." No mystery, no intrigue.

"Happening" — Straightforward and plain. "Something is happening." No implication of secrecy or significance.

"Brewing" — Suggests something is quietly developing, often negative — like a storm brewing. Similar feeling to "afoot" but leans more toward trouble.

"Afoot" stands apart because it uniquely combines the idea of active progress with a hint of drama, mystery, or significance. It tells you not just that something is happening, but that you should pay attention — something noteworthy is in motion.

Afoot (adjective, predicate only) = currently happening or being planned, often with a sense that it is significant, secretive, or noteworthy.

The golden pattern: "Something [linking verb] afoot" — and whatever that something is, it is not sitting still. It is moving. It is in progress. And it usually matters.
